newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook-Price could threaten four-year low.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook-Price could threaten four-year low.

text.p: Gold prices look to be heading southward and the lowest values since 1993 or even beyond are looming, dealers and analysts said.

"It is much easier to see reasons for the price going down than it going up," one analyst said, reflecting a sentiment that prevailed at the Financial Times Gold Conference in Prague at the beginning of last week and in market-wide dealings afterwards.
On February 12 the gold price fell to its lowest fixing since April 13, 1993 of $336.90 and on Monday morning that price looked under threat.
Gold was trading at $337.25/$337.75, having slipped under the apparently firm support level at $340.00.
Dealers said the market could continue to slip on a combination of a stronger dollar, weakening demand and speculator selling.
"It does not look good for the medium term," one London-based analyst said.

One reason the price was slipping off the precarious balance it held around $340.00 per ounce during most of May and June was that demand for physical metal traditionally turns down during the northern hemisphere summer season.
"Gold consumption was extraordinary good during the first four months of the year but its is definitely dropping off now," said an executive at a leading European refiner.
"It will probably stay like this for the next three months," he added.

Despite an overwhelmingly bearish outlook, involving the apparently increased threat of central bank gold sales and little guarantee that physical offtake would manage to outstrip mine supply, prices were reasonably stable last week.
Even so, on Friday the fix was at a four-month low of $338.20 per ounce and the short-term forecasts were less than favourable.
On Wednesday evening the Belgian government announced it planned to sell about 26 tonnes of gold per year in commemorative coin form for five years, possibly beginning in 1999.
The market lost $2 before finding support, but dealers and analysts said this was just another blow which an already punch-drunk market had to absorb.
"The head of the (Belgian) central bank said they would not sell again but now the government is saying they will. They've changed the rules," an analyst said.
The Belgian news, although not involving a huge a mount of metal and not immediately threatening, was just the latest in a string of bearish developments.

Less than a week before a discussion paper produced on behalf of the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank suggested there was no benefit in central banks holding gold in their reserves and the metal should be sold.
The central banks hold about 28,000 tonnes of gold, equivalent to about 12 years of new mine supply.
The paper suggested that the impact on the market would be to stop miners selling gold and reduce the price by about $41 per ounce from a notional $350.00 starting point.

"There was only a nominal reaction to this because the market is too tired after the Bundesbank and the Swiss (both planning to revalue their gold reserves) shocked it earlier this year," an analyst said.
